narrative: Fire ecology and climate change dominate today's strongest findings. In Conservation Biology, researchers document how Australia's 2019/2020 Black Summer bushfires drove rapid, collaborative biodiversity-focused emergency response, while a separate analysis of the Pantanal shows hydroclimatic disruption is expanding fire seasons and fire size across the world's largest wetland. Climate pressure surfaces repeatedly: European mountain flora shows surprising resilience despite compositional shifts, mature beech forests show drought responses that vary along regional gradients and differ among admixed species, and experimental evolution reveals that warming temperatures can leave lasting genomic signatures on evolving parasites. Movement ecology contributes two large-scale connectivity assessments -- jaguar corridors across the Americas and multi-species corridors for tigers, leopards and elephants in southern India -- both aimed at prioritising fragmented habitat for large-mammal conservation. In the trophic and symbiosis space, biological invasions are shown to disrupt size-spectrum relationships in freshwater fish communities, while dark septate endophytes are found to colonise winter wheat roots more heavily than arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi. Landscape-scale work highlights a trade-off: large-scale peatland rewetting in Germany boosts habitat heterogeneity but sharply reduces pollinator abundance, underscoring how restoration design choices carry ecological costs. Finally, a Science paper traces the temperate Eurasian origins of the woolly rhinoceros through Pleistocene paleogenomics, offering a rare deep-time perspective among today's largely contemporary ecological findings.
